texts: Hollow Creek woke to the smell of a butcher's barrel left out in the sun. It was coming from everywhere at once.
Something painted the church door last night, and it didn't use paint. The handprints went all the way up to the bell tower.
At midnight the rats came up out of every cellar in town and ran for the woods. Rats know.
All night, the sound of wet chewing came through the walls on Main Street. Nobody got up to look. Nobody wanted to.
At dawn the well bucket came up full of hair, with teeth rattling around in the bottom.
The moon was so red last night that the shadows looked wet. By morning, some of them were.
The wolves took someone apart slowly, starting at the feet, so the screaming would last. By the time they reached the belly, the screaming had turned to begging. They ate that part too.

Someone was sharpening a bone saw by candlelight when the pack came through the wall. They peeled the skin off in long wet strips and fought over the meat underneath like dogs over a bone. The skull was cracked open on the hearthstones and licked clean.

The wolves dragged someone out by the ankles, fingernails tearing off on the floorboards as they clawed for something to hold. Out in the yard, the pack opened the belly and pulled everything out while their victim was still breathing.
Someone's face was gone. Not torn, not bitten. Gone, eaten down to the grinning bone, while the rest of the body lay almost untouched in bed.
The pack hung someone from the barn rafters by their own intestines and took turns leaping up to tear off whatever they could reach. By morning only the top half was still swinging.
The vampire opened someone at the throat, both wrists and both thighs, and drank from each until it ran dry. What was left was folded into the bathtub like an empty wineskin, gray and crackling.
Someone was cleaning a meat hook in the rain barrel when the vampire found them. It bit through the cheek to reach the vein under the eye and drank while its victim watched with the other one.
They found someone hanging upside down from the church bell, slit from groin to chin, with buckets set underneath. The buckets were empty. The vampire had been thirsty.

The Witch's brew turned someone's blood to something like hot tar. The veins swelled black and split open under the skin, and the last hour of the night was spent picking pieces of flesh off the bedsheets.

Someone drank the potion thinking it was medicine. By midnight the teeth were floating loose in their mouth, the eyes had gone milky and runny, and the stomach had eaten its way through to the floorboards.
Whatever the Witch slipped into someone's tea made them claw at their own skin until they found bone. They were still scratching when the heart finally quit.
The Huntress pinned someone to an oak with arrows through both hands and both feet, then sat on a stump to watch. She only put the last arrow through the throat when she got hungry for breakfast.
Her first arrow went through someone's jaw and nailed the tongue to the roof of the mouth, so there was no screaming. The next nine arrows were just for fun.
The dying Hunter fired from flat on their back, guts spilling into the dirt. The arrow went through someone's eye, through the brain and out the back of the skull with a wet pop.
The Hunter's last arrow caught someone in the belly and tore it open sideways. They ran, trying to stuff everything back in with both hands, and made it almost to the well.

Under the lantern, someone's skin split down the spine and the wolf inside started climbing out, wet and steaming. The mob hacked at both halves with axes until neither one moved, then salted the pieces and burned them.

The Revealer's light caught someone half changed, jaw stretching and cracking, fur pushing up through bleeding skin. The blacksmith caved its head in with a sledgehammer, and the crowd kept swinging long after the twitching stopped.
The Revealer pointed at the wrong neighbor, and the dark came for someone instead. It turned them inside out, slowly, and left them on the doorstep like a wet red glove.
The shadows dragged someone up the chimney. Pieces came down all night. The last one to fall was the heart, still beating.
The Chupacabra drilled into someone's spine and drank the marrow straight from the bones. When the farmers lifted the body, it folded in half like an empty sack.

Someone was mixing something foul from the apothecary's back shelf when the Chupacabra came. It sucked out the eyes first, then the tongue, then everything else through the holes, until only a stiff, hollow husk was left.
The wolf bite had gone black and soft and full of worms, and tonight the rot reached someone's heart. They died screaming, pulling out handfuls of their own rotten flesh.
Someone's bitten arm had swollen to twice its size. Last night it burst like an overripe melon, spraying rot and maggots across the room, and they drowned in it.
Someone was found sitting at the kitchen table with their own eyes in the soup bowl, spoon still in hand. The chair across the table was warm.
Something had sewn someone's mouth shut from the inside. The body was found in bed, swollen with screams that never got out.

Someone found their lover's head on a fence post, pulled it down and rocked it until their own heart tore apart in their chest. Blood ran from their mouth onto their lover's face. They died of heartbreak.
Someone clawed into their lover's fresh grave with bare hands, fingernails peeling back, and lay down beside the body. The heart burst sometime before dawn. They died of heartbreak.
Without its companion, the Dire Wolf chewed through its own leg, then its own belly, howling the whole time. Someone was found curled in a pool of its own insides.
The Dire Wolf ripped out its own throat when its companion fell. Someone bled out in great pulsing gushes across the frost.
The Mad Bomber's blast turned someone inside out. Ribs were found in the church steeple, a hand in the bakery oven, and teeth buried in the mayor's front door.
When the Mad Bomber went off, someone was close enough to wear most of it. They lived for almost a minute afterward, which was the worst part.
Someone was counting stolen teeth by lantern light, and by morning only the skin was left, folded neatly on the porch like laundry. Nobody knows where the rest went.
Something dragged someone into the swamp by the hair. The water boiled red for an hour, then bones started floating up, picked clean and scratched with tiny teeth.
Someone was sharpening a bone saw by candlelight when something got them. The body turned up in the smokehouse, gutted and hung on a hook beside the hams, already cured.
The undertaker needed three buckets and a rake. He found the wedding ring in a pile of wolf droppings behind the church.
The pack had dragged the spine through the cornfield like a chew toy. The red trail runs all the way to the woods.
Somebody had dosed the evening ale with a sleeping powder, so they were out cold for the start of it. The neighbors swear they woke up for the end.
A meat cleaver lay on the floor with fur stuck to the blade, so they had fought. The pack ate the hand that held it first, then came back for the arm.
The priest drove a stake through the corpse just in case. Old black blood oozed up around the wood, and the body sat up and screamed once before it went still.
The vampire had numbed them with something sweet first, so they lay there smiling while it drank. The smile is still frozen on the shriveled gray face.
The healer opened the body to see what happened, and the smell knocked her flat. The insides had melted together into one black, bubbling lump.
Every rat that licked the bedsheets was dead by noon. The sheets were burned, and the ashes smoked green for a week.
She took her arrows back afterward, pulling them through instead of out. The holes were big enough to see daylight through.
Both bodies lay in the same field, the Hunter's guts steaming in the frost. The crows started with the eyes, as crows do.
The ashes kept twitching in the fire pit for an hour afterward. Nobody slept that night.
The Revealer found the leftovers in their own bed the next morning, still warm. Someone had written one word on the wall above it, in red: WRONG.
The farmers burned the husk, and it went up with a sound like a scream. Two of them breathed the smoke and coughed up blood for a week.
The doctor had been feeding them his strongest painkilling drops all week, and they did nothing. He burned the mattress and the floorboards under it.
Every clock in the house stopped at the same minute. Black water dripped from the ceiling onto the body all day.
They were buried together. The gravedigger swears the dirt moved for an hour afterward, like something underneath was still holding on.
Nobody wanted to touch the body, so they burned the whole shed down around it. It howled once more in the fire.
They're still finding pieces in the rain barrels. The baker found a finger in a loaf of bread and closed the bakery for good.
A rusty bone saw lay nearby, next to an empty little vial that smelled like bitter almonds. Whoever did this took their time, and took souvenirs.
The undertaker took one look, drank a whole bottle of the apothecary's strongest tincture, and walked into the river. They're still looking for him too.
The sheriff threw up, wiped his mouth, and threw up again. He's burning his boots behind the jail and won't say what he stepped in.
By noon the crows were so fat on the leftovers they couldn't fly. They sat on the fence, beaks dripping, staring at everyone who walked past.
They laid a sheet over the body, and it soaked through in seconds. Then something underneath the sheet sighed.

Every animal in Hollow Creek was opened up last night. The cows were turned inside out, the horses were nailed to the barn doors by their hooves, and the chickens were plucked alive. Every person is still breathing. They won't be for long.
The streets are slick with blood this morning, ankle-deep in some places, but every person in Hollow Creek is accounted for. Nobody knows whose blood it is. Nobody wants to know.
Someone woke up this morning in a puddle of blood that wasn't theirs, with claw marks gouged into the floor an inch from their throat. Something stopped the beast. Just barely.
There's a severed wolf paw nailed to one door this morning, still twitching. Someone fought back last night and lived to see the sun.
The mob held the accused down in the town square and went at them with a bone saw, starting at the knees and working up. They took turns, so everyone got a go.
They boiled the accused alive in the big iron soup pot behind the church. The screaming went on until the skin slid off, and the soup went to the pigs.
The village strapped the accused to the old wagon wheel and turned it one notch for every vote against them. The joints went first, one by one, with sounds like green wood snapping. Then the spine.
They buried the accused up to the neck in the square, poured honey over their head and kicked open the anthill. It took until sundown. The ants were not quick.
The crowd tied the accused to the mill wheel and opened the sluice. Every turn dragged them under the grinding stone. By evening, the flour coming out of the mill was pink.
The blacksmith heated his tongs until they glowed and went to work on the accused while the whole town watched. When they finally dragged what was left to the gallows, it was a mercy.

The blade had already taken one of the accused's fingers when they screamed, "I am the Prince!" and held up the royal seal in a bloody hand. The crowd backed away. Nobody wants to explain this to the king.

The noose was already tight when the accused started giggling and drooling blood from a bitten tongue. The crowd lost its stomach and cut them down. The Village Idiot lives, minus a few teeth, but their vote doesn't count anymore.
The vote split, and the arguing turned into an axe fight in the square. Two villagers lost hands, one lost an eye and the blacksmith lost an ear, but the gallows stayed empty.
The rope was ready, the axe was sharp and the pot was boiling, but not enough of you wanted blood today. The crowd went home starving.
Nobody accused anyone today. Somewhere in the crowd, a wolf ran its tongue over its teeth and counted the hours until dark.
Afterward the butcher hung what was left on the meat hooks outside his shop as a warning. The flies found it before the crowd had even gone home.
Half the crowd had been passing around a jug of something strong and bitter since noon. A few of them took pieces home as keepsakes, and nobody stopped them.
The head went up on a pike at the town gate. By morning the crows had taken the eyes, and the mouth was full of beetles.
The body was dumped down the old dry well. Some mornings, the bucket still comes up with fingernails in it.

Someone fought through the mob to their lover's torn-up body and screamed until something in their chest ripped loose. Blood poured from their mouth and nose. They died of a broken heart, right on top of their lover.
A Dire Wolf smelled its companion's blood on the wind, tore its own belly open with its claws, and bled out howling.
That body belonged to the Mad Bomber. It went off like a powder keg, and someone was standing close enough to catch most of it. They lived for almost a minute afterward.
Someone collapsed in the crowd, coughing up blood, and died.

As the last light faded, an old wolf bite on someone in the crowd split open, and what poured out was black and crawling with maggots. They'd been rotting on their feet all day. They collapsed screaming and clawed at the wound until their heart gave out.

The instant the accusation was seconded, someone's skin split along every vein at once. The vampire's bite had been working on them all night. They collapsed in front of the whole village, skin folding over bone, as the last of their blood hissed out onto the cobblestones.
Whatever rot was festering in that body, the wolves swallowed it whole. They spent the night vomiting blood, fur and pieces of their own stomachs behind the church. No hunting tonight.
The pack found their cub's body split open. The mother wolf ate her pup's heart to keep it with her, then howled until the windows cracked. Tonight they take two of you, and they'll make it last.
The Troublemaker has whipped the village into a frenzy. One body won't be enough today. Two of you must be voted out before sundown.

The village caught the last wolf alive. They skinned it in the square while it screamed, nailed the hide over the gate and roasted the rest on a spit. Hollow Creek ate well that night, and nobody asked what it tasted like.
When the last villager stopped screaming, the pack lay down in the town square on a bed of bones and slept with full bellies. Hollow Creek is nothing now but a larder.
The vampires hung the last villagers by their ankles in the church and drained them one by one, slowly, savoring every drop. The pews are stained black, and the town is silent forever.
The last two lovers waded through the blood in the square, stepping over everyone they ever knew, and kissed under the red moon. They are the only things left breathing in Hollow Creek.
The Tanner choked on their own blood, eyes bulging, laughing through it the whole time. Dying was exactly the plan. Everyone else loses.
It's over. Nothing in Hollow Creek is left alive except the flies, and the flies are very, very happy.

The noose was already around the accused's neck when someone shoved through the crowd and pulled it over their own head instead. Nobody stopped them. The trapdoor dropped, and the rope did what ropes do.
Someone stepped between the accused and the mob's axes and spread their arms wide. The first blow was meant for someone else. The mob didn't bother to stop for the rest.
